title: 6 days Pull Push Legs program review
summary: NH reviews a viewer's (Japjit Singh's) 6-day pull/push/legs program and calls it minimalism done right, with good rep ranges and a strength hook on each day. He discusses Pendlay rows, pull-up form, face pulls, Nippard shrugs, RDLs versus hamstring curls, superset options, and how the order of days affects deadlift/squat recovery.
claims: Push/pull/legs is the worst ordering of the three-day split; putting push in the middle (pull/push/legs) or starting with legs is better
1x4-6 is an excellent deadlift prescription; heavy floor pulls need little frequency because other lower and upper body lifts already feed them tonnage
You still need to practise the deadlift, because training within its exact specificity is the best way to progress on it
4-6 reps is the upper end for deadlifts, where mechanical failure starts to matter
Opening a pull day with a heavy floor pull is the best strength work you can do, because it trains and warms up the whole body
Do warm-up sets before heavy rows after deadlifts, because jumping straight into heavy elbow flexion risks tendon injury
Pairing deadlifts and triceps on the same day shows no understanding of programming
Pendlay rows (dead stop from the floor every rep, negative not controlled) are the toughest rows; 6-8 reps suits them
Experiment with grip and touch point on Pendlay rows (hips, belly button, solar plexus), but don't row high to the chest, where shoulder flexion gets dangerous
Rowing lower emphasises the rhomboids; rowing to the solar plexus brings in more upper back, traps and rear delts
Horizontal rows rank fairly low among movement patterns but are great for posture and teach holding a neutral spine
Pendlay rows don't belong in novice programs; novices can't even pull from the floor with good form
Pull-ups are usually best done for max reps, but 6-8 reps just shy of failure works well because vertical pulls return to baseline easily
On pull-ups, don't fully extend at the bottom, which disengages the lats; the top is shoulder flexion, so forcing your head over the bar wastes energy
15-20 reps is perfect for face pulls; they prevent rear delt imbalance, are non-invasive and quick to set up, and are easy to recover from
Flat barbell bench 3x4-6 is effectively a 3x5 with an evolving range, and it is the best horizontal press
The military press could handle more volume, such as an extra set
Incline and decline presses work better with dumbbells, flat horizontal presses with a barbell
Push days need long-head triceps work like overhead extensions; most presses don't train it
Nippard shrugs progress very fast; 2 sets of 12-15 gives plenty of stimulus
Most people on push/pull or upper/lower programs are really writing a body part split without calling it one
The traps stabilise the shoulders, so tire them at the end of a push day; some powerlifters avoid back work before a big bench day for this reason
Don't superset pull-ups with hammer curls since both tax the grip; pair face pulls with either instead
Chin-ups can be supersetted with military press on push day without taking away strength
Long-head triceps work does not hurt pressing much, but test this with incline/decline presses
Three sets of Nippard shrugs is doable and four is pushing it; it is a partial cheat shrug, so treat it as trap isolation, not strength work, and don't chase load
He always front squats for 5 reps because thoracic extension limits higher reps, though 6-8 as a back squat accessory is fine
Hamstring curls mostly hit the lower hamstring and back of the knee, causing knee pain with poor form; RDLs hit the glute-hamstring tie-in and carry over to the deadlift, so he prefers RDLs
Lifters who lack flexibility compensate with the lumbar spine on hamstring curls, which is why some get lower back pain from them
4x8-12 is the best rep range for RDLs, which allow unmatched grinding
Calves need high volume; 4x12-15 is excellent
The weighted decline crunch is his favourite ab exercise: stretch fully, add weight over time; it builds the abs and decompresses the spine
The program is minimalism done right: 15% more would be too much and 15% less too little for progression
Shrugs every three days are all traps need, especially alongside deadlifts and face pulls
Deadlifts don't tax him but squats do: he can deadlift heavy then squat two days later, but not the reverse
If heavy squats hurt the next day's deadlift, switch to pull/push/legs/rest repeated
exercises: dead stop from floor each rep; touch hips, belly or solar plexus, not high chest
don't fully extend at bottom; don't force head over bar
rear delt and trap balance, non-invasive
long head work missing from presses
trap isolation that progresses fast; not strength work
isolates lower hamstring; knee/back pain with poor form
full stretch at bottom, all the way up, add weight
